newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German bank sector rocked by mega-merger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German bank sector rocked by mega-merger.

text.p: The reformation of Germany's bank sector began on Monday when two Bavarian banks unveiled a bold plan to merge into a German banking giant second only to the mighty Deutsche Bank AG.

Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechselbank AG, both Bavarian specialists in mortgage lending and ranked fourth and fifth respectively among listed commercial banks, said they would merge as equal partners to form Bayerische Hypo- und Vereinsbank AG.

The new bank will be a powerful force in German banking, a sector seen as ripe for consolidation, with combined assets of 743 billion marks ($416 billion), toppling Dresdner Bank AG, the number two, and not far off Deutsche, which in 1996 had total assets of 886 billion marks.

It will concentrate on retail banking, property finance and asset management and will be Europe's leading mortgage bank, the banks said, adding that it will not shy away from foreign acquisitions to strengthen its investment banking business.
"I think it is not an exaggeration to say that this is the realisation of a vision in Europe's banking market," Hypo-Bank chairman Eberhard Martini told a news conference.

"Hypo-Bank and Vereinsbank alone are too small to realise the economies of scale which are necessary on the enlarged market. By merging they have reached a volume which will enable them to remain competitive and to act autonomously in the future European market."

The stock market's focus is now likely to shift to other potential merger candidates, heightening what had already been intense interest in bank shares. "The Gordian knot has been cut," one analyst said, predicting further mergers.
Analysts gave the merger a mixed reception, calling it a first major step towards consolidation in a market seen as hopelessly overbanked but doubted whether the bank would shed enough jobs.

Polticians welcomed what they termed the "Bavarian solution" which they said would safeguard jobs, enhance the status of fiercely independent Munich as a financial centre, and keep out the big Frankfurt rivals Deutsche and Dresdner which had been seen as possible predators.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, head of Bavaria's CSU party, said: "The decision is right and positive for Munich as a financial centre." He said politicians would now have to put pressure on the two banks to minimise job cuts.
Investors also gave the plans a firm thumbs-up, sending the two banks' share prices to all-time highs.
Vereinsbank shares, which have nearly doubled on merger talk in the past year, rose 3.4 percent to 85.70 while Hypo-Bank jumped 14 percent to 66.70 marks, having earlier traded as high as 74 marks.
Under the deal, Vereinsbank will swap four-fifths of its 10 percent stake in insurer Allianz AG for shares in Hypo-Bank, offering one Allianz share for six Hypo-Bank shares.
That values Hypo-Bank shares at 75 marks, giving a 28 percent premium on the closing price of 58.50 marks on July 18.
Vereinsbank will thereby obtain up to 45 percent of Hypo-Bank. After the swap Vereinsbank will raise capital by a nominal 150 million marks to boost the new bank's equity base.
The merger will be prepared from October and terms for the linkup will be based on 1997 final results. The deal will be presented to shareholders for approval by spring 1998.
The German cartel office must also approve the deal but analysts said this was unlikely to be problematic.

The merger is expected to cost around 1.3 billion marks in restructuring costs but the banks said it would also cut expenses by as much as one billion marks per year in five years and spark a "marked increase" in earnings.
The new bank should reach a return on equity of 15 percent after tax before the year 2000.

Vereinsbank chairman Albrecht Schmidt and Hypo-Bank's Martini, both of whom have said they are available to head up the new bank, refused on Monday to specify how many jobs of a combined 40,000 would be shed.

"We're not embarking on a cost defensive but on a quality offensive," Schmidt said. "We need every hardworking and qualified man and woman on board our larger ship in order to make progress on this stormy world market."
Martini conceded there were strong overlaps between the banks but said both have reduced staff in recent years and that branch closures would lead to better staffing levels at the branches remaining.
The banks together had staff turnover of 2,000 employees per year, Martini said. That meant any job cuts could be carried out in a "very gentle and socially acceptable way."

Analysts had mixed views of the plan. Commerzbank immediately raised its recommendation on the top five listed German banking stocks to a "buy", while Salomon reduced its recommendation on Vereinsbank to "hold" from "buy".
Salomon analyst Matthew Czepliewicz said he was concerned that the new bank would not be able to achieve its earnings goals because of political pressure not to shed too many jobs.
Expectations that the financial services sector was on the brink of a shake-up gained fresh currency in recent weeks after news of a merger of two insurers under Munich Re.
Rumours had been rife that a major deal was underfoot since last August, when Deutsche Bank triggered merger frenzy by announcing it had a 5.2 percent stake in Vereinsbank.

The rationale behind mergers is clear. Germany is regarded as heavily overbanked with more than 3,600 commercial, public and cooperative banks battling for market share, and a rate of one branch per 1,100 inhabitants.
The top five banks, led by Deutsche, have a joint market share of just 14 percent and are struggling to make their costly retail branch networks more efficient.
Dresdner, which could have merged with Hypo-Bank under one of the alternative scenarios, said it did not expect the merger to disrupt its strategic links to Allianz.

Deutsche gave a cautious welcome to the plans, terming its stake in Vereinsbank "a good investment". Viag, which indirectly owns 10.24 percent of Vereinsbank, said it would retain its stake in the bank. ($ = 1.787 German Marks)
